en: Dīgha Nikāya 24: Pāṭikasutta 1. The Account of Sunakkhatta I have heard that on one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, at the Gabled Hall. Then the wanderer Pāṭika approached the Blessed One and, having approached, exchanged greetings with him. When they had concluded their polite and amiable conversation, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, the wanderer Pāṭika said to the Blessed One: “Master Gotama, the ascetic Gotama says this: ‘There is no other ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees as I do. Master Gotama, what does he say by this? “Pāṭika, when I say, ‘There is no other ascetic or brahmin who knows and sees as I do,’ I say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the past, the future, and the present. “But, Master Gotama, how is it that you say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the past?

“Pāṭika, I know of beings who, with the breakup of the body after death, have reappeared in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell; and I know of beings who, with the breakup of the body after death, have reappeared in the heavenly world. And I know the details of how these beings were in the past, and how they have fared according to their deeds. It is in this way, Pāṭika, that I say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the past. “But, Master Gotama, how is it that you say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the future? “Pāṭika, I know of beings who, with the breakup of the body after death, will reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell; and I know of beings who, with the breakup of the body after death, will reappear in the heavenly world. And I know the details of how these beings will fare according to their deeds. It is in this way, Pāṭika, that I say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the future. “But, Master Gotama, how is it that you say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the present? “Pāṭika, I know of beings who are possessed of bodily misconduct, verbal misconduct, and mental misconduct, who revile noble ones, hold wrong views, and perform actions based on wrong views. I know that with the breakup of the body after death, such beings will reappear in states of deprivation, in an unhappy destination, in perdition, even in hell. And I know of beings who are possessed of good bodily conduct, good verbal conduct, and good mental conduct, who do not revile noble ones, hold right views, and perform actions based on right views. I know that with the breakup of the body after death, such beings will reappear in the heavenly world. It is in this way, Pāṭika, that I say this with reference to the knowledge and vision regarding the present. When this was said, the wanderer Pāṭika said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Master Gotama, it is marvelous! How the Venerable Gotama knows himself! Thus have I heard:
at one time the Blessed One was staying among the Mallas at a town of the Mallas named Anupiya.
Then, in the morning, the Blessed One dressed, took his bowl and robe, and entered Anupiya for alms.
Then it occurred to the Blessed One:
“It is still too early to wander for alms in Anupiya.
What if I were to go to the park of the wanderer Bhaggava-gotta, where the wanderer Bhaggava-gotta is?”
Then the Blessed One went to the park of the wanderer Bhaggava-gotta, where the wanderer Bhaggava-gotta was staying.
Then the wanderer Bhaggava-gotta said this to the Blessed One:
"Welcome, venerable sir; welcome, venerable sir."
“Welcome, venerable sir, to the Blessed One.
It has been long indeed, venerable sir, since the Blessed One last made the occasion to come here.
Let the Blessed One sit down; this seat is prepared.”
The Blessed One sat down on the prepared seat.
The wanderer of the Bhaggava clan also took a certain low seat and sat down to one side.
Sitting there, the wanderer of the Bhaggava clan said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, some days ago, even earlier than that, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi came to me and said:
‘Bhaggava, I have now renounced the Blessed One.
I shall no longer live as one who dwells under the guidance of the Blessed One.’”
“Is it really so, Bhante, as Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son said?
“It is exactly so, Bhaggava, as Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son said.
Several days ago, Bhaggava, several days earlier, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me.”
Having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side.
Seated to one side, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son said this to me:
"Venerable sir, I now renounce the Blessed One."
‘Venerable sir, I shall no longer live as one supported by the Blessed One.
When this was said, Bhaggava, I said this to Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis:
‘Did I ever say such a thing to you, Sunakkhatta?’”
“Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell depending on me,” did you say that to me?
“Certainly not, Bhante.
“Or did you say this to me?”
‘Venerable sir, shall I dwell supported by the Blessed One?
‘Certainly not, venerable sir.
‘In that case, Sunakkhatta, it seems I do not say this to you:’
"Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell under my patronage. "I do not say to you,
'Venerable sir, I shall dwell under the Blessed One's patronage,'" he replied.
“This being so, foolish man, who are you that you reject whom?
Look, foolish man, at how far you have gone astray!
“But, Bhante, it is not that the Blessed One performs for me a superhuman feat of psychic power,” he said.
“Sunakkhatta, did I ever say to you:
‘Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell under me; I will perform for you a superhuman feat of psychic power’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Or did you say this to me:
‘Venerable sir, I shall live depending upon the Blessed One; the Blessed One will perform for me a superhuman feat of psychic power’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
"Thus indeed, Sunakkhatta, it was not that I said to you:
'Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell under my guidance; I will perform for you a superhuman feat of psychic power as a miracle';
nor did you say to me: [I will dwell under your guidance]."
"Venerable sir, I shall dwell depending upon the Blessed One, thinking: 'The Blessed One will perform for me a superhuman feat of psychic power.
"If that is so, you foolish man, who are you and whom do you reject?
What do you think, Sunakkhatta?"
“Whether a superhuman feat of psychic power has been performed or not, does the Dhamma for which I have taught the Dhamma lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering?
“Venerable sir, whether a superhuman feat of psychic power has been performed or not,
the Dhamma for which the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.”
‘Thus indeed, Sunakkhatta, whether a superhuman feat of psychic power has been performed or not,
the Dhamma has been taught by me for the purpose that it leads the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.’
“In that case, Sunakkhatta, what further miracle of supernormal power beyond human capacity could possibly be performed?
Look, you foolish man, how far you have gone astray!
“But, Bhante, does the Blessed One not proclaim the origin of the world? “No, Sunakkhatta, I do not proclaim the origin of the world.”
“Sunakkhatta, did I ever say to you:
‘Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell under my guidance; I will explain to you the primordial origin’?
“Certainly not, Bhante.”
“Or did you say this to me:
‘Venerable sir, I shall live under the Blessed One’s guidance; the Blessed One will explain the first principle to me’?
“Certainly not, venerable sir.”
“Thus indeed, Sunakkhatta, it was not that I said to you:
‘Come, Sunakkhatta, dwell under me; I will proclaim to you the first principle.
Nor indeed did you say to me:”
"Venerable sir, I shall dwell depending upon the Blessed One, thinking: 'The Blessed One will explain the ultimate origin to me.
This being so, you foolish man, who are you and whom do you reject?
What do you think, Sunakkhatta?"
“Whether the first point has been laid down or not laid down, does the Dhamma for which I have taught the Dhamma lead one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering?
“Whether the first point has been laid down, Bhante, or not laid down, the Dhamma for which the Blessed One has taught the Dhamma leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.

“So it seems, Sunakkhatta, whether the first point has been laid down or not laid down, the Dhamma for which I have taught the Dhamma leads one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.”
In that case, Sunakkhatta, what will your proclamation of the "primordial beginning" achieve?
Look, you foolish man, how far you have gone astray!
In many ways, Sunakkhatta, you have spoken in praise of me in Vajjigāma.

"Such indeed is the Blessed One: an arahant, perfectly enlightened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of the worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of gods and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One.
In this way, Sunakkhatta, you have praised me in many ways in the Vajjian village.
And in many ways, Sunakkhatta, you have praised the Dhamma in the Vajjian village.
"The Dhamma has been well-expounded by the Blessed One; it is visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, and to be realized by the wise for themselves.
Thus, Sunakkhatta, have you spoken in many ways in praise of the Dhamma in the Vajjian capital.
And thus, Sunakkhatta, have you spoken in many ways in praise of the Saṅgha in the Vajjian capital.
The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced well; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced uprightly; the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced methodically;

the Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples has practiced with propriety—namely, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of offerings, worthy of hospitality...
“Worthy of offerings, worthy of salutation with joined palms, an unsurpassed field of merit for the world.
Thus, Sunakkhatta, have you spoken in many ways in praise of the Saṅgha in Vajjigāma.
I declare this to you, Sunakkhatta; I make this known to you, Sunakkhatta.

“Sunakkhatta, there will indeed be those who will say of you: ‘Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son was not able to lead the holy life under the ascetic Gotama; being unable to do so, he abandoned the training and returned to the lower life.
Thus, Sunakkhatta, there will be those who will speak of you.
In this way, Bhaggava, though addressed by me in such a manner, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son departed from this Dhamma and Discipline, like one bound for a state of misery and hell.
2. The Story of the Kṣatriya of Kora.
"Once, Bhaggava, I was staying at Thūlū, a market town of the Thūlūs called Uttaraka.
Then, Bhaggava, having dressed in the morning and taken my bowl and robe, I entered Uttaraka for alms with Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, as my attendant monk."
Now at that time, Bhaggava, the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya, who followed the dog-vow, was eating food scattered on the ground with his mouth alone, consuming it with his mouth alone.
Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis, saw the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya, who followed the dog-vow, eating food scattered on the ground with his mouth alone, consuming it with his mouth alone.
Having seen him, this thought occurred to him:
‘“How excellent indeed is this ascetic! He eats his food scattered on the ground from four bowls with nothing but his mouth; he consumes it with nothing but his mouth!
Then, Bhaggava, having known with my own mind the reflection that had arisen in the mind of Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son, I said to him:
‘You too, you foolish man, claim to be an ascetic, a son of the Sakyan?’”
“But, Bhante, why does the Blessed One say this to me:
‘How can you, foolish man, claim to be a recluse, a son of the Sakyans?

“Did it not occur to you, Sunakkhatta, after seeing this naked ascetic Korakkhattiya—who follows the dog-vow, who uses four bowls, and who eats food scattered on the ground, eating with his mouth and consuming with his mouth—did it not occur to you:”
“‘How excellent indeed is this ascetic! He eats with his four hands, consuming food scattered on the ground with his mouth alone, eating with his mouth alone!
‘It is so, Bhante.
But why, Bhante, does the Blessed One begrudge the attainment of arahantship?’”
“Foolish man, I do not begrudge you the state of arahantship.
However, this evil speculative view has arisen in you; abandon it!
Let it not lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.”
As for this man, Sunakkhatta, whom you think of as the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya—"This ascetic is a person of great worth"—he will die of dysentery on the seventh day.
Having died, he will be reborn among the asuras called Kālakañjas, the lowest class of asuras.
And when he has died, they will cast him away upon the Bīraṇa-grass heap in the charnel ground.
And if you wish, Sunakkhatta, you should approach the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya and ask him:
"Friend Korakkhattiya, do you know your own destination?
It is possible, Sunakkhatta, that the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya will give you an answer.
“I know my own destination, friend Sunakkhatta:
I have been reborn among the asuras called Kālakañjas, the most inferior class of asuras.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya; having approached him, he said this to the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya:
“Friend Korakkhattiya, you have been declared by the ascetic Gotama:
‘The naked Korakkhattiya will die of indigestion on the seventh day.
Having died, he will be reborn among the asuras called Kālakañjakas, the lowest class of asuras.’”
"And when he has passed away, they will cast him away on a charnel ground at the Bīraṇa-thicket.
Therefore, friend Korakkhattiya, you should eat food in moderation and drink water in moderation,
so that the ascetic Gotama’s word may prove false."
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son counted each day for seven nights and days, as one who did not believe in the Tathāgata.
Then, Bhaggava, on the seventh day, the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya died of dysentery.
Having died, he was reborn among the asuras known as Kālakañjakas, the most inferior class of asuras.
And when he had passed away, they abandoned him at the Bīraṇa-thicket cemetery.
Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son heard:
“The naked ascetic Korakkhattiya has indeed died of dysentery and has been abandoned at the Bīraṇa-thicket cemetery.”

Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son went to the Bīraṇa-thicket charnel ground where the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya was; having approached him, he struck the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya three times with his hand, saying:
“Do you know, friend Korakkhattiya, your own destination?
Then, Bhaggava, the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya arose, rubbing his back with his hand.
“I know my destination, friend Sunakkhatta,” he said.
“I have been reborn among the Asuras known as the Kālakañjakas, the most wretched class of Asuras. Having said this, he fell down right there on his back.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me; having approached, [he spoke].
Having paid homage to me, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Bhaggava, I said this to Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis:
"What do you think, Sunakkhatta?"
“Sunakkhatta, do you consider that the result for the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya was exactly as I predicted when I spoke concerning him, or was it otherwise?
“Venerable sir, the result for the naked ascetic Korakkhattiya was exactly as the Blessed One predicted; it was not otherwise.
“What do you think, Sunakkhatta?”
“If this were so, would a superhuman feat of psychic power have been performed, or not?
“Certainly, Bhante, if this were so, a superhuman feat of psychic power would have been performed; it would not be unperformed.
“Even though I was performing a superhuman feat of psychic power, you, foolish man, speak to me in this way.”
"But it is not because the Blessed One, Bhante, does not perform a further miracle of supernormal power beyond human dhamma for me," [he said].
"Behold, you foolish man, how far you have gone astray!
Thus, Bhaggava, even though Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son was spoken to by me in this way, he departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya, like one bound for the states of deprivation, destined for hell.
3. The Account of the Naked Ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka “Bhaggava, on one occasion I was dwelling at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka was residing at Vesālī in the Vajjian village, having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame.”
He had undertaken seven vows: “For as long as life lasts, I shall be naked and not wear clothes;

for as long as life lasts, I shall live a celibate life and not engage in sexual intercourse; for as long as life lasts, I shall subsist only on raw grain and meat, and not eat boiled rice or cooked gruel;
to the east of Vesālī, I shall not pass beyond the Udena Shrine; to the south of Vesālī, [I shall not pass beyond] the Gotamaka Shrine...”
‘I shall not cross the Cāpāla Shrine to the east of Vesālī; I shall not cross the Sattamba Shrine to the west of Vesālī;
I shall not cross the Bahuputta Shrine to the north of Vesālī.
By virtue of undertaking these seven rules of conduct, he attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame in the Vajjian village.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka; having approached him, he asked the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka a question.
When the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka was asked the question, he could not answer it.
Being unable to answer, he manifested anger, hatred, and resentment.
Then, Bhaggava, it occurred to Sunakkhatta, the son of the Licchavis:
"Alas, we have indeed insulted a truly noble Arahant ascetic!
May this not lead to our harm and suffering for a long time!"
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Bhaggava, I said this to Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son:
“‘Even you, foolish man, will claim to be a recluse, a son of the Sakyan?
‘But why, venerable sir, does the Blessed One say to me:
“Even you, foolish man, will claim to be a recluse, a son of the Sakyan”?’”
“Did you not, Sunakkhatta, approach the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka and ask him a question?
When he was asked that question by you, the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka was unable to answer it.
Being unable to answer, he manifested anger, hatred, and resentment.”
Then this occurred to him:
"Alas, we have insulted a truly noble arahant ascetic!
May it not lead to our harm and suffering for a long time!"
“Yes, venerable sir.
But why, venerable sir, does the Blessed One begrudge arahantship?
“I do not begrudge arahantship, foolish man.”
Moreover, this evil course of view has arisen in you;
abandon it, lest it lead to your harm and suffering for a long time.
As for that naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka whom you think of, Sunakkhatta—

"This ascetic is a man of good character," [he thought]. But before long, that naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka, clothed in fine robes and wandering about with attendants, eating boiled rice and sour gruel, passed beyond all the shrines of Vesālī and, his reputation diminished, he died.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son heard:

‘The naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka, it seems, having been clothed and living with his followers, eating boiled rice and sour gruel, has passed beyond all the shrines of Vesālī and died fallen from his fame.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there, Bhaggava, I said to Sunakkhatta:
I said this to the son of the Licchavis:
“What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
Is the outcome exactly as I declared concerning the naked ascetic Kālāmaṭṭaka, or is it otherwise?”
“Venerable sir, just as the Blessed One has explained concerning the naked ascetic Kaḷāramaṭṭaka, so will its result be, and not otherwise.
“What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
If this is so, has a superhuman feat of psychic power been performed, or has it not?”
“Certainly, Bhante, when this is so, a superhuman feat of psychic power has been performed, not one that has not been performed.
“In this way too, you foolish man, while I am actually performing a superhuman feat of psychic power, you say of me:
‘But, Bhante, the Blessed One does not perform a superhuman feat of psychic power for me.’”
"Behold, you foolish man, how far you have gone astray!
Even though I spoke thus to Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, Bhaggava, he nevertheless departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya, like one bound for a state of misery, destined for hell.
4. The Account of the Naked Ascetic Pāṭikaputta.
Once, Bhaggava, I was staying right there at Vesālī in the Great Wood, in the Gabled Hall.
Now at that time, the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta was residing at Vesālī, having attained the pinnacle of gain and the pinnacle of fame in the Vajjian village.
He spoke these words in an assembly at Vesālī:
‘The ascetic Gotama is a proponent of knowledge, and I too am a proponent of knowledge.
Indeed, one who is a proponent of knowledge deserves to display a marvel of psychic power beyond human reach to another who is a proponent of knowledge.
Let the ascetic Gotama come halfway along the road, and I too shall go halfway along the road.’
There, both of us together shall perform a superhuman feat of psychic power (*iddhi-pāṭihāriya*).
If the ascetic Gotama performs one superhuman feat of psychic power, I shall perform two;
if the ascetic Gotama performs two superhuman feats of psychic power, I shall perform four.

‘If the ascetic Gotama performs four wonders of supernormal power beyond the human state, I shall perform eight. Thus, for however much the ascetic Gotama performs a wonder of supernormal power beyond the human state, I shall perform twice as much, twice over. Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me; having approached, [The remainder of the passage follows: ...he stood to one side and said to me: ‘Venerable sir, I am going away from the ascetic Gotama. I have no further use for the ascetic Gotama. When this was said, I told him: ‘But, Sunakkhatta, have you not seen anything in me, or heard anything from me, that you are going away from me? ‘Venerable sir, I have seen nothing in you, nor have I heard anything from you, that I am going away from you. But rather, it is because of my lack of faith in your superhuman states and qualities that I am going away from you. ‘But, Sunakkhatta, do you have faith in the superhuman states and qualities of those ascetics and brahmins who have passed away? "What if I were to make my lair in dependence upon a certain grove?
Having made my lair there, I would emerge from my lair in the evening; having emerged from my lair, I would stretch out;
having stretched out, I would look around in the four directions; and having looked around in the four directions, three times..."
"I shall let out a lion’s roar; having roared the lion’s roar three times, I shall go forth for my prey.
Having slain the choicest of the deer herd and eaten the tenderest of the tender meats, I shall return to that very same lair.
Then, friend, that old jackal made his lair near a certain woodland thicket.
Having made his lair there, he emerged from his lair in the evening; having emerged from his lair, he stretched;

having stretched, he looked around in the four directions; and having looked around in the four directions, thinking, "I shall roar three times the lion’s roar," he did not even bark like a jackal, nor did he howl like a jackal, [saying]: "What are these wretched jackals? What indeed is this 'lion's roar'?"

"In the same way, friend Pāṭikaputta, while living on the alms of the Sugata and consuming the remnants of the Sugata, you think it appropriate to insult the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
But who is this wretched Pāṭikaputta, and what is his power to insult the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?
When, Bhaggava, Jāliya the pupil of Dārupattika was unable by this parable to move the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta from his seat, [he remained silent].
Then he said this to him:
"Beholding himself as a lion,
the jackal imagined, 'I am the king of beasts.'"
"In the same way, you bark like a jackal at the lion’s roar:
'Who is this lowly jackal? Who is this roaring the lion’s roar?

Even so, friend Pāṭikaputta, while living on the footprints of the Sugata and consuming the remnants of the Sugata, you think you can challenge the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones."
"And who is Pāṭikaputta? And what is the provocation against the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?
But since, Bhaggava, Jāliya Dārupattikantevāsī was unable even by this parable to move the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta from his seat, he then said this to him:
“Another’s path he follows,
while looking at himself for his own sustenance;
as long as he does not see himself...”
The jackal, for its part, thinks, "This is a tiger. In that same way, it does not even bark at a jackal,
saying, "What is this wretched jackal, and what is this lion's roar?"
"In the same way, friend Pāṭikaputta, while living on the alms of the Sugata and eating the remnants of the Sugata, you think you can insult the Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
But who is this wretched Pāṭikaputta, and what is the insult to the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?
But even with this simile, Bhaggava, Jāliya the wood-carver’s pupil was unable to move the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta from his seat.
Then he said this to him:
“Having eaten frogs, field mice,
and corpses cast away in burial grounds;”
Having grown up in the great forest, in the empty forest,
the jackal imagined, "I am the king of beasts";
likewise, he barked at a dog.
“What kind of wretched jackal is this, and what kind of lion’s roar?

Even so, friend Pāṭikaputta, while living on the footprints of the Sugata and consuming the remnants of the Sugata, you imagine yourself able to challenge the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones.
What kind of wretched Pāṭikaputta are you, and what kind of challenge is this to the Tathāgatas, the Arahants, the Perfectly Enlightened Ones?”
But since, Bhaggava, Jāliya Dārupattikantevāsī was unable even with this simile to move the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta from his seat, he went to that assembly and announced:
“Sirs, the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta is ruined! ‘I am coming, friends! I am coming, friends! he says, yet he writhes right there; he cannot even rise from his seat.”
When this was said, Bhaggava, I said to that assembly:
"Friends, the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta is incapable of coming into my presence without first abandoning that speech, abandoning that mind, and relinquishing that view.
Even if it were to occur to him thus—"

"If I were to go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama without having abandoned that speech, without having abandoned that mind, and without having relinquished that view, my head would surely split apart.
Even if it were to occur to the venerable Licchavis,
'Let us bind the naked Pāṭikaputta with thongs and drag him along with elephants,' those thongs would either break or Pāṭikaputta would [break free]."
“However, Pāṭikaputta the naked ascetic is incapable of coming into my presence without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that state of mind, and without relinquishing that view.

Even if he were to think, ‘I will go into the presence of the ascetic Gotama without abandoning that speech, without abandoning that state of mind, and without relinquishing that view,’ his head would surely split apart.
Then, Bhaggava, I instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened that assembly with a discourse on the Dhamma.

I gladdened that assembly; having instructed, exhorted, inspired, and gladdened them with a discourse on the Dhamma, I effected their release from the great bondage and rescued eighty-four thousand beings from the great abyss.
Then, entering the fire-element, I rose into the air to the height of seven palm trees, and another seven palm trees further up, amidst a mass of flames.
Having manifested this, having blazed up, and having emitted smoke, I reappeared in the Gabled Hall in the Great Forest.
Then, Bhaggava, Sunakkhatta the Licchavi son approached me;
having approached and paid homage to me, he sat down to one side. As he was sitting there to one side, Bhaggava, I [addressed] Sunakkhatta...
I said this to the son of the Licchavis:
“What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
Is the result exactly as I declared concerning the naked ascetic Pāṭikaputta, or is it otherwise?”
“Venerable sir, just as the Blessed One has declared concerning Acela Pāṭikaputta, so too will that be its result, and not otherwise.
“What do you think, Sunakkhatta?
If this is so, has a superhuman feat of psychic power been performed, or has it not?”
“Certainly, Bhante, if that were so, then a superhuman feat of psychic power would have been performed, not one unperformed.
“In this way too, you foolish man, while I was performing a superhuman feat of psychic power, you said of me:
‘But, Bhante, the Blessed One does not perform a superhuman feat of psychic power.’”
"Behold, foolish man, how far you have gone astray!
Even though I spoke thus to Sunakkhatta, son of the Licchavis, Bhaggava, he nevertheless departed from this Dhamma and Vinaya, like one bound for a state of misery, destined for hell.
6. The Discourse on the Exposition of the Origin of the World (Aggañña-paññatti-kathā)
“Bhaggava, I understand the theory of origins (*aggañña*).

I understand it, and I understand what is even higher than that; and understanding it, I do not misapprehend it. For one who does not misapprehend it, personal extinction (*nibbuti*) is known by me, such that when a Tathāgata realizes it, he does not fall into ruin.
Bhaggava, there are certain recluses and brahmins who proclaim a theory of origins based on the teachings of Īśvara and Brahmā as their teacher.”
I approached them and said this:
“Is it true, venerable sirs, that you proclaim the primordial beginning as being based on the work of Īśvara, the work of Brahmā, and the teaching of a teacher?
When questioned by me in this way, they admitted, “Yes.”
I say this to them:
“In what way, venerable sirs, do you prescribe the primordial beginning consisting of the acts of Īśvara, the acts of Brahmā, and the teacher’s tradition?
When questioned by me in this way, they are unable to answer; being unable to answer, they question me in return.
When asked about them, I explain:
"Friends, there comes a time, after the passing of a long period, when this world contracts.
When the world is contracting, beings for the most part are reborn in the Ābhassara realm."
There they dwell, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, abiding in beauty, remaining for a very long time indeed.
Now, friends, there comes a time, after the passing of a long period, when this world expands.
As the world expands, an empty Brahma-palace appears.
Then, a certain being, through the exhaustion of his lifespan or the exhaustion of his merit, passes away from the Ābhassara realm and is reborn in an empty Brahma palace.
There he dwells, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, established in beauty, and remains for a long, extended period of time.
Because he has lived there alone for a long time, dissatisfaction and agitation arise within him.
"O, would that other beings too might come to this state!

Then, through the exhaustion of their lifespan or the exhaustion of their merit, other beings pass away from the Ābhassara realm and are reborn in the empty Brahma-mansion to be the companions of that being.
There they dwell, mind-made, feeding on rapture, self-luminous, moving through the air, abiding in beauty, and remaining for a very long time.
In this regard, friends, the being who was the first to be reborn there thinks:

"I am Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Vanquisher, the Unvanquished, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that has been and will be. By me were these beings created. And why is that?"
For previously this thought occurred to me:
"O, may other beings too come to this state! Such was my mental aspiration, and now these beings have indeed come to this state.
And those beings who were reborn later also think:

"This, indeed, is the Lord Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Sovereign, the Maker, the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that has been and will be;
we have been created by this Lord Brahmā."
For what reason?
Because we saw that he was the first to be reborn here, while we were reborn later.
In that case, friends, the being who was reborn first has a longer life span, is more beautiful, and possesses greater influence than those reborn later.
But those beings who were reborn later are shorter-lived, more ugly, and less influential.
Now, friends, it is possible that a certain being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state of existence, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, through ardor, through striving,
through application, through diligence, and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that,
with his mind thus concentrated, he recollects his past lives; beyond that, however, he does not recollect.
Thus he spoke: "That venerable Brahmā, the Great Brahmā, the Conqueror, the Unconquered, the All-Seeing, the All-Powerful, the Lord, the Maker,
the Creator, the Chief, the Ordainer, the Father of all that have been and shall be— by whom we were created by the venerable Brahmā..."
‘He is permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, remaining exactly the same for all eternity.
But we who were created by that venerable Brahmā are impermanent, unstable, short-lived, subject to fall, and have come to this state of existence.
Thus, venerable sirs, do you prescribe this doctrine of the creation by God (Issara), the creation by Brahmā, as a teacher’s tradition, as the origin of all things.”
They said this:
“It is even so, friend Gotama, as we have heard it, just as the venerable Gotama has said.
And I, Bhaggava, understand the origin of the world.

I understand that, and I understand what is superior to it; and understanding that, I do not cling to it. And for me, through non-clinging, personal coolness is realized. That which the Tathāgata directly knows, he does not fall into misfortune because of it.
Bhaggava, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim a primordial beginning based on a teacher’s tradition corrupted by indulgence in play.
Having approached them, I say this to them:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you proclaim the origin of the world based on the corruption of pleasure as your teacher’s tradition?
When I have asked them this, they acknowledge, ‘It is so.
I then say to them:
"But in what way, venerable sirs, do you prescribe this tradition concerning the origin of the world as corrupted by pleasure?
When I questioned them thus, they were unable to answer; being unable to answer, they questioned me in return, and when I was questioned by them, I explained:
“Friends, there are gods called ‘Corrupted by Play. They dwell excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight.
As they dwell thus excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight, their mindfulness fails them;
through the loss of mindfulness, those gods fall away from that host.”
But it is possible, friends, that some being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state;
having come to this state, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness;
and having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, through ardor, through exertion, and through application...
Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he recollects his past lives, but does not recollect beyond that.
He says this:
“Those venerable devas who are not corrupted by play do not dwell excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight.
Because they do not dwell excessively devoted to the nature of laughter, play, and delight, their mindfulness does not fade away;
through the non-forgetting of mindfulness, those devas do not fall from that host.”
"They are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly so for all eternity.
But as for us, who were once corrupted by play— dwelling excessively devoted to the nature of laughter,
play, and pleasure— while we dwelt thus excessively devoted to laughter, play, and pleasure, our mindfulness was lost."
‘Through a lapse of mindfulness we have thus passed away from that body;
being impermanent, unstable, short-lived, and subject to falling away, we have come to this state.
Venerable sirs, you prescribe such a tradition of yours, corrupted by pleasure, as the beginning of all things.”
They said this:
“It is indeed so, friend Gotama; we have heard it exactly as the venerable Gotama has spoken.
And I, Bhaggava, understand the first beginning of things... [as before] ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [as before].
"Because of what he directly knows, the Tathāgata does not fall into error.
Bhaggava, there are some recluses and brahmins who proclaim a primordial beginning based on a teacher’s tradition of mental corruption.
Having approached them, I say this to them:"
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you proclaim this primordial beginning based on malice of mind as your teacher’s tradition?
When I have asked them this, they admit, ‘It is so.
To them I say:
"But how, venerable sirs, do you prescribe this primordial beginning characterized by mental corruption as your teacher's tradition?
When questioned by me in this way, they were unable to provide an answer; being unable to answer, they instead questioned me in return.
To them, when questioned, I replied:
“Friends, there are gods called ‘Mind-Defiled. They gaze excessively upon one another.
Gazing excessively upon one another, they become corrupt in mind toward each other. With minds corrupted toward one another, their bodies grow weary and their minds grow weary.
Those gods pass away from that host.”
But it is possible, friend, that some being, having passed away from that body, comes to this state of existence.
Having come to this state of existence, he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the household life into homelessness, through ardor, through exertion, and through application...
Through diligence and through right attention, he attains such a concentration of mind that, with his mind thus concentrated,
he recollects his former lives, but does not recollect beyond that.
He says this:
“Those venerable devas who are not corrupt in mind do not gaze excessively upon one another.
Because they do not gaze excessively upon one another, they do not harbor ill will toward one another.
With minds free from ill will toward one another, their bodies are unwearied and their minds are unwearied. Those devas do not pass away from that host.”
“They are permanent, stable, eternal, not subject to change, and will remain exactly so for all eternity.
But we, who were corrupted in mind, dwelt upon one another excessively.
By dwelling upon one another excessively, we corrupted our minds toward one another. We—”
“With minds corrupted toward one another, our bodies exhausted and our minds exhausted,
we have passed away from that realm and, being impermanent, unstable, short-lived, and subject to falling away, have come to this state of existence.
“In this way, venerable sirs, you proclaim an origin of the world based on mental corruption as your teacher’s tradition.”
They said this to me:
“It is indeed so, friend Gotama; we have heard it exactly as the venerable Gotama has spoken.
And I, Bhaggava, understand the origin of the world... [and so on].
Because of what the Tathāgata directly knows, he does not fall into error.
Bhaggava, there are some ascetics and brahmins who proclaim a doctrine of origins based on fortuitous origination as their teacher’s tradition.
Having approached them, I say this to them:
‘Is it true, venerable sirs, that you proclaim a doctrine of origins based on chance as the teacher’s tradition?
When they are asked this by me, they admit, ‘It is so.
To them I say:
"But how, venerable sirs, do you prescribe this doctrine of the origin of the world as having arisen fortuitously?
When questioned by me in this way, they were unable to provide an answer; being unable to answer, they instead questioned me in return.
To them, when questioned, I replied:
“Friends, there are gods called the Non-percipient Beings.
With the arising of perception, those gods pass away from that plane.
It is possible, friends, that some being, having passed away from that plane, comes to this state of existence.”
Having come to this state, he goes forth from the home life into homelessness.
Having gone forth from the home life into homelessness, through ardor, through striving, through application, through diligence, and through right attention,
he attains such a concentration of mind that, when his mind is thus concentrated...
He recalls that arising of perception in his mind, but does not recall anything beyond that.
He says this:
‘The self and the world have arisen by chance.’
"And for what reason?
Because previously I did not exist, and now, having not existed, I have undergone transformation into a state of being.
"In this manner, do you venerable ones proclaim your doctrine of the origin of the world as having arisen by chance?"
They said this to him:
“It is indeed so, friend Gotama, as the venerable Gotama has spoken.

“Bhaggava, I understand the origin of the world; I understand it, and I understand what is even higher than that. Understanding it, I do not cling to it. And for me, through non-clinging, personal liberation is realized.”
"Because the Tathāgata knows this, he does not fall into error.
Bhaggava, when I speak thus and declare this, certain recluses and brahmins falsely, vainly, and untruthfully misrepresent me with what is non-existent, saying:
"The recluse Gotama and his monks are perverted."
"The ascetic Gotama says thus:
'At whatever time one enters and dwells in the liberation of the beautiful, at that time one understands everything as indeed unattractive.
But I, Bhaggava, do not speak in this way."
‘At whatever time one dwells having attained the beautiful liberation, at that time one understands everything as indeed unattractive.
Yet, Bhaggava, I say this:
‘At whatever time one dwells having attained the beautiful liberation, at that time one understands it as indeed beautiful.’”
“But those, venerable sir, who perceive the Blessed One erroneously and the bhikkhus as well, are themselves mistaken.
I am so confident, venerable sir, in the Blessed One that the Blessed One is capable of teaching me the Dhamma in such a way that I might enter upon and abide in the liberation of the beautiful.

“However, Bhaggava, it is difficult for you—who hold a different view, who accept a different doctrine, who find pleasure in a different doctrine, who apply yourself to a different practice, and who follow a different teacher—to enter upon and abide in the liberation of the beautiful.”
“Come now, Bhaggava, you should properly preserve this very confidence that you have in me.

“If it is difficult for me, Bhante, being of another view, of another inclination, of another preference, with a different application, and a different teacher, to enter and dwell in the beautiful liberation— nevertheless, Bhante,
I shall properly preserve this very confidence that I have in the Blessed One.”
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The wanderer of the Bhaggava clan, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The first sutta, the Pāṭika-sutta, is finished.
